clinicalPearls: A distinctive granulomatous variant of rosacea characterised by firm, monomorphic yellow-brown to red papules and nodules on a relatively normal-appearing background
Lesions favour the cheeks, perioral and periocular skin and may extend beyond the usual convexities of the central face
In contrast to classical rosacea, the flushing, background erythema and telangiectasia may be minimal or absent
Diascopy of the papules can reveal an apple-jelly appearance similar to other granulomatous facial dermatoses
Histology shows dermal epithelioid granulomata, sometimes with caseation-like necrosis, which can cause confusion with tuberculosis
The condition overlaps clinically and histologically with lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei, and their relationship remains debated
It tends to be more persistent and treatment-resistant than ordinary rosacea, and healing may leave scarring

Management follows rosacea principles with prolonged courses of oral tetracyclines, topical agents and treatment of any demodex contribution, avoiding potent topical corticosteroids which aggravate the disease
reference.pathophysiology: Granulomatous rosacea is regarded as a granulomatous tissue reaction pattern occurring within the spectrum of rosacea. As in other rosacea subtypes, dysregulation of the innate immune system, an abnormal cutaneous vascular and neurovascular response, and an inflammatory reaction to Demodex mites and their microbial load are thought to contribute. In this variant the inflammatory response organises into dermal epithelioid granulomata around follicular structures, sometimes with central necrosis, producing the characteristic firm papules. The precise trigger for granuloma formation is unclear, and the histological picture can closely resemble that of lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei and cutaneous tuberculosis.
additionalDifferentials: Perioral (periorificial) dermatitis, including its granulomatous form
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy to confirm dermal granulomata and characterise any necrosis
Special stains and culture to exclude mycobacterial and fungal infection
Skin scrapings or biopsy assessment of Demodex density
Investigations to exclude sarcoidosis when granulomata are found (e.g. chest imaging)
Clinical review of prior topical corticosteroid use as an aggravating factor
Assessment for ocular rosacea when periocular lesions are present
redFlags: Granulomatous histology that could represent cutaneous tuberculosis or sarcoidosis requiring systemic evaluation
Progressive scarring or disfiguring facial involvement
Failure to respond to appropriate rosacea therapy, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Granulomatous rosacea often runs a chronic and relatively treatment-resistant course requiring prolonged therapy, and although many patients eventually improve, residual scarring or persistent papules can occur.
pitfalls: Prescribing potent topical corticosteroids, which characteristically worsen the eruption
Misinterpreting necrotising granulomata as proof of tuberculosis without confirmatory microbiology
Expecting rapid resolution and stopping treatment prematurely
Failing to distinguish it from sarcoidosis and missing systemic disease
references: British Association of Dermatologists rosacea guidance
management: Use oral tetracyclines such as doxycycline for their anti-inflammatory effect as first-line systemic therapy
Apply topical agents including metronidazole, azelaic acid or ivermectin, the last also reducing Demodex load
Reserve oral isotretinoin for disease resistant to antibiotics
Withdraw any topical corticosteroid, which aggravates the condition
Advise general rosacea trigger avoidance and photoprotection
Assess for and treat coexisting ocular rosacea, particularly with periocular lesions
Refer to dermatology and counsel that the course is often chronic and treatment-resistant with risk of residual scarring
